sentenceSets.sentence: The poet's attention to euphony made the lines pleasurable to read aloud even before their meaning fully registered.

answerChoices.reasoning: Rhythm concerns the pattern of stresses in time, but the sentence credits the pleasure to how the lines strike the ear when voiced, which a metrically regular line full of harsh consonants would fail to deliver.
Diction is the choice of words for sense and register, while the sentence says the pleasure arrives before the meaning does, locating it in sound rather than in word choice.
Cadence describes the fall and shape of a phrase in time, and the sentence points to the sweetness of the sounds themselves rather than to their pacing.
Rhyme is the matching of end sounds at set positions, whereas the sentence attributes the pleasure to the whole texture of the lines as spoken.
Clarity is a virtue of meaning, and the sentence explicitly says the pleasure came before meaning had registered.
Imagery works through pictures the reader forms, which again belongs to the sense the sentence sets aside.
Brevity is a matter of length and would not make lines pleasurable in the mouth.
Syntax is the arrangement of grammar, and a well-built sentence can still sound ugly aloud.
Cacophony is harsh sound, the opposite of what makes the lines a pleasure to speak.
Silence cannot be what makes lines rewarding to read aloud.
Obscurity is a fault of sense and would not produce pleasure in the reading voice.

sentenceSets.sentence: Choosing a name for the company, they settled on one whose euphony survived being said quickly by a tired receptionist.

answerChoices.reasoning: Brevity would help a tired receptionist too, but the test described is how the name holds up as sound when spoken fast, not how few syllables it has.
Clarity concerns being understood, whereas the criterion the sentence applies is whether the name still sounds good under rapid speech.
Memorability is about what a listener retains afterward, while the test here happens in the moment of the receptionist saying it.
Dignity concerns the impression of seriousness a name gives, and the sentence's trial is an acoustic one conducted at speed.
Spelling is a written property and would not be tested by anyone saying the name aloud.
Originality distinguishes the name from competitors and has nothing to do with surviving hurried pronunciation.
Accuracy would concern whether the name describes the business, not how it sounds at the front desk.
Length is a measurable feature but not one that can survive or fail to survive being spoken.
Harshness is the very quality a name chosen for its sound would be avoiding.
Illegibility is a defect of writing and is irrelevant to a spoken test.
Cost has no bearing on how a name sounds when said quickly.

sentenceSets.sentence: The dialect coach prized euphony over accuracy, softening consonants that a real farmhand from the county would have snapped off.

answerChoices.reasoning: Elegance covers refinement of any kind, while the specific change described is to consonants, which is an adjustment to how the speech sounds in the ear.
Intelligibility would be about audiences following the words, but the coach's softening of consonants risks blurring them rather than making them clearer.
Authenticity is what the sentence says was sacrificed, since the real farmhand's harder consonants were the accurate version.
Projection is carrying the voice to the back of the house, and softening consonants would work against being heard at distance.
Volume is loudness, which is untouched by whether consonants are snapped off or softened.
Diction as an actor's crispness of articulation is precisely what the coach is sanding down.
Pacing concerns speed of delivery, and the alteration described is to the consonants themselves.
Grammar governs word forms and order, not the hardness of a consonant.
Harshness is what the real farmhand's snapped consonants supply and what the coach is removing.
Silence cannot be prized in a discussion of how consonants are pronounced.
Stammering is a disfluency no coach would prize over accuracy.
